To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the initial eradication of an introduced predator, the cat, from Little Barrier Island, led to the counterintuative decline of the breeding productivity of the endemic Cook's petrel, a native species, which is vulnerable to predation from a mesopreditor, the Pacific rat, and that rat eradication was followed, after a lag period of about 10 years, by an increase in the breeding productivity of Cook's petrel.

the removal of a top predator from Little Barrier Island, New Zealand, resulted in a decline in Cook's petrel productivity due to the ecological release of a mesopredatory species, the Pacific rat, and that this mesopredator impact was spatially heterogeneous across the landscape.

the eradication of cats from an oceanic island led to the release of a smaller introduced predator, which in turn reduced the productivity of a native prey species in a process called mesopredator-release.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how introduced predators affect the population dynamics of a seabird and how the effects of predator eradication on prey populations vary across an oceanic island.
the spatial heterogeneity of meso-predator release within predator prey communities on Little Barrier Island.
the effects of predator removal on the population dynamics of a native seabird species.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the removal of a top predator (cats) from Little Barrier Island resulted in a mesopredatory species, the rat (Rattus exulans) becoming the dominant predator.
the eradication of introduced predators from islands may not be a straightforward solution for the conservation of native fauna and flora.
Spatial heterogeneity of introduced predator impacts on island ecosystems may be driven by environmental gradients that interact with introduced species to produce counterintuitive outcomes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the eradication of introduced species is a complex and often counterintuitive process that can have unexpected consequences for native species.

mesopredator releases can occur in island ecosystems and can be spatially heterogeneous, and that the outcomes of such mesopredator responses are dependent on the spatial distribution of the mesopredator and prey populations, as well as environmental gradients.

mesopredator effects on prey are spatially heterogeneous and can vary over time, and thus, the outcomes of predator eradications may not be predictable without a detailed understanding of the ecological interactions between predators and prey.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the outcomes of predator eradications can vary across space and time.
the effects of predator removal on prey populations may be spatially heterogeneous.
the impacts of predator removals on native prey can be highly variable and depend on the presence of other predators.
